Data centers are now a midterm issue, even in Brooklyn
articles.description: At a Brooklyn midterm party five days before Election Day, every conversation, from a council member’s fireside chat to a debate about the Democratic Party, kept circling back to AI and data centers.
articles.content: On Thursday evening, I slipped on my neon yellow heels and a floral mini dress. It’s New York, so I can wear whatever I want to a midterm election event full of media types, techies, policy advocates, and, well, does anyone else even exist at these things? I walked into the dimly blue-lit Brooklyn warehouse and was surprised to see the room already filling up. Newsreel, the media company founded by former Forbes and Newsweek reporter Jack Brewster, hosted the event, and the lineup was heavy-hitting. Kenneth Schlenker, co-founder of the focus app Opal, sat down for a fireside chat about “the state of attention,” and Aryan Banjan, who built the campaign management software Barza, gave a midterm forecast. I, meanwhile, was moderating a panel on data centers. Brewster said the goal was for people to “put their phones away and talk to each other about the election, five days out.” As the evening progressed, however, one topic consumed nearly every conversation: AI, data centers, and the backlash against the growing technocracy. Lately, as a tech reporter, I’ve noticed a growing chasm between tech and everyone else. I spend most of my days talking to people who see the benefits of AI, who are so ambitious in building it and so optimistic that it will succeed that, when I talk to people beyond the tech world, I forget how ugly it all seems to them. Outside the tech bubble, data centers and AI have become such an intense ballot-box issue that they could sway some midterm races on November 3. A recent report from Data Center Watch found that almost $200 billion in data center projects were delayed, stalled, or blocked in the first half of 2026 due to political and community opposition. Meanwhile, states like Pennsylvania, Georgia, Texas, New York, and Virginia are considering more guardrails and transparency around data centers’ rapid development. Hundreds of new data centers are planned in Virginia alone, a state already nicknamed the “data center capital of the world.” A fireside chat with New York City Council member Chi Ossé, just before my panel, set the tone. AI came up near the end; Ossé said he doesn’t really use it. To me, though, he didn’t seem to be for or against it. He mostly emphasized that he would like to see tech executives held more accountable and trillionaires like Elon Musk taxed more. He described himself as a democratic socialist, but a “law and order” one. When CEOs talk about a technology that could deplete 10% of human civilization, he said, “they should be called to testify in front of Congress.” My panel was up next. I moderated a discussion with Maia Woluchem, a technology and human rights researcher, and Hilary Flint, an environmental and public health advocate, about data centers. As I took the stage, I decided to get a better read on the crowd. I asked, “Who here is pro-AI data center?” and was promptly booed. Our conversation covered a range of topics and emotions. People are upset that big tech companies appear to be cutting secret deals with local officials to build billion-dollar data centers. In some cases, zoning rules make it unclear what is being built until it’s too late to protest. At the same time, people are struggling with the cost of living and doing everything they can to hold onto what’s left of the American Dream, while tech leaders talk about AI replacing workers, or even humanity itself. Residents feel they have lost control over what happens in their communities, and they worry about the environmental and health risks. The panel agreed that data centers are the physical embodiment of people’s fears and anger toward the tech class and the rapid pace of technology. “What is a life worth?” Flint said when I brought up the benefits that some communities have seen from data center build-outs. People still protest, she said, because they “value their lives a little bit more than a temporary check.” The panel after mine featured NewsNation host Batya Ungar-Sargon; political strategist Morris Katz, who worked on Zohran Mamdani’s campaign; and Vox’s Astead Herndon. They were supposed to be talking about the future of the Democratic Party. But once again, the conversation shifted to data centers. Ungar-Sargon noted that some labor unions support data centers because of the jobs they promise. (Reports show that data centers create many jobs initially, but those jobs are not permanent once construction ends.) “There used to be a lot of pride in a community in the Rust Belt about very ugly, enormous buildings in their communities because everybody worked there,” she said, nodding to an earlier comment I’d made about data centers being ugly. “And they knew that building represented prosperity for themselves, stability for their children, and a future and a piece of the American dream.” Herndon noted that Vivek Ramaswamy was booed for making a similar point in Ohio, a Rust Belt state. “I just want to reinforce the lack of consent happening,” he said. “Because that’s true among Republicans in those places and I’ve watched it.” Katz was also skeptical. “It’s the same people who have taken so many union jobs away,” he said. “The same institutional powers that have robbed labor and working people of jobs and profit. Now coming back to essentially finish the job and take whatever scraps remain.” Along the warehouse walls, I noticed sticky notes answering posted questions, including “Will we ever be able to get Big Money out of politics?” “God, I hope so,” one note said. People rushed the bar when the panel ended, and techno music began to blast. They broke into small groups, where AI and data centers were once again the topic, this time in more private conversations. I asked Brewster if he was surprised by how much of the conversation focused on AI and data centers. “It came up in every conversation on stage, and it was the second most common topic in the questions people sent us when they RSVP’d,” he said, adding that it was happening even in New York, where data centers aren’t very visible. “AI has become an election issue for regular voters,” he said. “In rural communities, the backlash is about feeling replaced. In a place like Brooklyn, it’s more about who gets rich from it.” Before leaving, I made the rounds, asking people to name the craziest thing they’d seen in tech this year. Two tech founders mentioned the AI assistant startup Instinct, while a non-tech person named Sam Altman Another non-tech person brought up the rise of deepfakes and AI art. AI art, she said, is starting to signal cheapness. That may be why luxury brands are going the other way: Prada’s holiday campaign features hand-drawn illustrations, and Hermès has been spotlighting artists’ handmade work on Instagram. On my way out, I spoke to a software engineer who said the craziest thing she’d seen this year was a person who painted their nails orange for Halloween and was asked if it was a tribute to the Anthropic IPO. I admitted that I, too, had once worn a burnt orange dress and briefly thought of myself as the Claude logo. She later told me data centers are popping up in her Southern California hometown, too. Hearing that, I thought for the first time about how I’d feel if one popped up in mine. She grew up in a Chinese immigrant community, where neighbors are putting signs in their yards showing dragons choking a data center. The signs have since been translated into other languages, she said. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. articles.description: Federal officials investigate arson at beleaguered police department in Mississippi AP News Federal officials investigate suspected arson at beleaguered police department in Mississippi CNN ATF, other agencies now investigating Senatobia Police Department fire as arson WREG.com Troubled police department catches fire amid fury over 1-year-old's killing and chief's racist texts The Independent Fire guts HQ of Miss. po
articles.content: An arson Saturday morning damaged the building of a beleaguered police department in Mississippi that has drawn outrage from the community in recent months after an officer shot and killed a 1-year-old, authorities said. It was unclear what caused the fire at the headquarters of the Senatobia Police Department. The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and local agencies are investigating. The Associated Press has reached out to the fire department, police department, and the Tate County Sheriff’s Office for comment. Firefighters were dispatched to the city’s police department at 4:58 a.m. to respond to smoke in the building, the Senatobia Fire Department said in a statement, and crews were able to quickly knock out the fire. There were no details on the damage. The Senatobia Police Department ignited anger in the community of 8,000 after an officer fired into a vehicle and killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley in June while investigating a shoplifting call at a Walmart. Wiley, who is Black, was in the vehicle with his mother, who was unharmed, and her friend, who was seriously injured. The two women denied having stolen anything, and no charges have been filed against them. In September, the police chief was fired after reporting by The New York Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News alleged that he used racist slurs in private text messages. Earlier this month, the officer involved in the shooting resigned, though he was cleared of criminal wrongdoing by the Mississippi Attorney General’s office after its probe concluded his use of force had been justified. Senatobia is about 40 miles (65 kilometers) south of Memphis.

US plans to deport Afghans back to their home country through Pakistan, documents show
articles.description: US plans to deport Afghans back to their home country through Pakistan, documents show AP News U.S. to Send Dozens Back to Afghanistan, Despite Risk of Persecution The New York Times Trump administration plans to deport some Afghan immigrants to Afghanistan Reuters Trump administration set to deport Afghan refugees to Pakistan, despite risk they’ll be returned to Taliban NBC News Afghans scheduled for deportation may
articles.content: President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to deport Afghans detained in the U.S. back to their home country via Pakistan, according to court documents obtained by The Associated Press — a move advocacy groups say could put their lives at risk. Immigrant rights organizations say those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban. Thousands fled persecution and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan. “This is absolutely unconscionable,” said Shawn VanDiver, a U.S. Navy veteran and president of the advocacy group #AfghanEvac. “It seems like there’s no end to their willingness to break the law and violate people’s human rights.” The U.S. intends to initially deport Afghan immigrants as early as Monday on flights from Louisiana, where the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency has immigrant detention and processing facilities, to Pakistan, according to court documents. The plan to deport Afghans to Pakistan was first reported by Bloomberg on Monday. On Friday, The New York Times reported that the immigrants were going to be sent to Afghanistan after arriving in Pakistan. A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in an email to the AP on Saturday that ICE does not comment on future immigrant-removal operations, citing operational security and personnel safety. Officials at the Pakistani Embassy in Washington did not immediately return email messages. U.S. officials confirmed the Afghan deportations in sealed court documents obtained by the AP. In a document filed in federal court in Virginia on Friday, a senior ICE official acknowledged that an Afghan immigrant had been scheduled to be on an upcoming charter flight from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Pakistan, “with further transport onward to Afghanistan.” The document was filed in the case of an immigrant who is not in custody and is challenging efforts to deport him. In another federal court case in Oklahoma, federal prosecutors filed a document on Monday disclosing that another Afghan immigrant was scheduled to be deported to Afghanistan sometime next week. The Trump administration has deported thousands of immigrants to countries other than their own. It has done this in some instances when it is unable to send them to their own countries because the US does not have formal relations, like with the Taliban government in Afghanistan. In other instances, it has been used as a deterrent. In many cases, a U.S. immigration judge has determined their lives would be in jeopardy if sent to their home countries. It was not immediately clear if any designated for return to Afghanistan have protective orders against being sent there. Human Rights First, an advocacy group for refugees and asylum seekers that tracks U.S. deportation flights, said Saturday that it had confirmed a scheduled flight from Louisiana to Pakistan on Tuesday carrying Afghan immigrants. “It is beyond egregious that this administration plans to carry out an unprecedented mass deportation flight of Afghans, forcibly sending them through Pakistan and into the hands of the Taliban,” Savitri Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights for Human Rights First, said in an email to the AP. “This follows previous unconscionable deportation flights we have tracked under this administration, including Iranian Christian converts and political dissidents removed via Qatar and Kuwait to Iran, as well as a Russian political dissident removed via Egypt to Russia,” Arvey said. Some Democratic members of Congress took to social media to criticize the Afghan deportations after seeing the Times story on Friday. “It is reprehensible that the Trump Administration plans to deport hundreds of Afghans, including women, children and those who supported U.S. forces, to Pakistan — who then risk being sent back into the hands of the Taliban. Congress must stand against this,” Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire posted on X. Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut added in his own X post, “We made a promise to our Afghan allies — that after aiding & protecting our troops during the conflict in Afghanistan, America would not abandon them. This Administration is betraying that promise, deporting them to potential torture & death.” In September, Trump’s administration finalized a last-minute reprieve to avoid the closure of a camp in Qatar that houses more than 1,000 Afghans who assisted America’s war effort or are the relatives of U.S. service members. The administration extended for nine months the life of Camp As Sayliyah, which had been due to close Sept. 30 at the end of the U.S. budget year. Upon entering his second term, Trump, a Republican, paused his Democratic predecessor’s Afghan resettlement program as part of a series of executive orders cracking down on immigration, including dramatically altering refugee admissions to focus on white South Africans. The refugee changes left thousands of people who fled war and persecution — and had gone through yearslong vetting processes to start new lives in America — stranded at places worldwide, including the base in Qatar.

articles.title: Haley Stevens advised to stay away from Abdul El-Sayed campaign events to limit ‘distractions’
articles.content: A public spat has cast Democratic tensions in the spotlight as the close US Senate race draws to a head Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s tightly fought US Senate race, wants Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens to stay away from his campaign events. “I don’t want any distractions,” El-Sayed told reporters after a campaign rally, according to the New York Times. “It seems as though other folks are more interested in making this race about things that it’s not about.” The two had planned to appear together on Sunday at a church service in Detroit, but Representative Debbie Dingell later told CNN she had spoken to Stevens and told her “This isn’t working.” Dingell added that the tensions between the two were a distraction and that “there’s nothing to be gained by the two of them being in the same place.” The public rupture between the progressive El-Sayed and the more moderate Stevens, whom he defeated in a bitter primary, has cast Democratic tensions into the spotlight in one of the most consequential elections in the party’s campaign to retake control of the Senate. Stevens endorsed El-Sayed shortly after he won the primary election in August, and planned to campaign with him on Sunday. But Stevens had until now avoided appearing publicly with her former opponent, whom she has criticized publicly for weeks. Her fiance, Jason Turkish, has campaigned on behalf of Republican candidate Mike Rogers. And just two days before they were scheduled to campaign together this weekend, Stevens demanded that El-Sayed denounce an outside group’s political ad that blamed higher prices on US support for Israel’s war in Gaza. “Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago,” El-Sayed shot back in a statement, which noted that the American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent heavily to defeat him in the primary. “Let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics, putting money in pockets, and passing Medicare for All,” the statement said. The open feuding worries many Democrats, who see the tight race as a must-win for the party to win back the Senate. “I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing,” Michigan state senator Mallory McMorrow told CNN Friday. “This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes. People are not talking about ads. They are not talking about Haley Stevens. They are talking about the price of gas and groceries.”

articles.content: To win a cross country regional, everything has to go right. It’s safe to say that everything went according to plan Saturday for Macomb Lutheran North and Holly’s cross country teams at Columbus County Park. Lutheran North landed five runners inside the top 35 and the Mustangs captured a Division 2 regional title with 68 points to punch their ticket for the Nov. 7 Lower Peninsula Division 2 state finals at Brooklyn’s Michigan Speedway. Birmingham Marian finished second with 83 points and Bloomfield Hills Cranbrook Kingswood grabbed the third and final state qualifying spot, as the top three teams and the top seven individuals not on the qualifying teams plus the entire top 15 medalists all advance to the state finals. Holly (101), Pontiac Notre Dame Prep (101), Yale (135), Armada (138), St. Clair (199), Croswell-Lexington (223), Marysville (233), Warren Regina (275), Orchard Lake St. Mary’s (324), St. Clair Shores Lake Shore (426) and Imlay City (435) were amongst the team left on the outside looking in at state qualifying berths. Beyond individuals in the top 10, Auburn Hills Avondale’s Lyla Eidson (12th), Croswell-Lexington’s Madelyn Barkley (14th) and Armada’s Claire Albrecht (15th) also qualified for state. articles.title: ICE agent charged with assault for hitting a fleeing man with his car will turn himself in on Monday
articles.description: ICE agent charged with assault for hitting a fleeing man with his car will turn himself in on Monday AP News Indicted ICE officer accused of intentionally striking man expected to surrender on Monday ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos Who is Mario 'Bam' Morales, the ICE agent behind the indictment? KHOU Search warrant identifies ICE agent who ran over man in Houston area Click2Houston ICE agent charged
articles.content: A federal immigration officer charged with aggravated assault after he ran over a Mexican man with his car in Houston will turn himself in on Monday, according to his attorney. Mario Alberto Morales, a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old construction worker, with his unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as he chased Parra Hernandez through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales on Friday on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Morales is planning to turn himself in at a courthouse sometime on Monday, David Lindenmuth, his attorney, told The Associated Press. Lindenmuth previously told the AP that the incident was “clearly just an accident” and that local officials had “invented a crime out of thin air.” Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told reporters on Friday. ICE has said Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales’ car. Previously released surveillance camera video shows Morales’ vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away. Teare played footage from Morales’ body camera on Friday that showed the agent making sharp turns with his steering wheel. He then stops and exits the vehicle and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is lying on the ground, screaming. “I was coming in, and I hit him with the car,” Morales can be heard saying after another ICE agent arrives. Parra Hernandez told deputies that he fled the traffic stop when Morales started pulling on a mask, and Morales “threw the car” at him, according to a Harris County Sheriff’s Office incident report reviewed by the AP. Morales told deputies that he did not brake before he hit Parra Hernandez, but that he did not intentionally strike him, according to the report. ICE said after the incident that the target of the operation was a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who the agency said was seen getting into a car with Parra Hernandez. Mendoza-Cervantes’ daughter told the immigrants’ rights group FIEL that her father has been dead for nearly a decade. Morales is among a small handful of federal agents who have been criminally charged for wounding people during the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown. ICE agent Christian Castro pleaded not guilty last month to charges that he lied to the FBI after he shot and wounded a Venezuelan man as immigration agents swept Minneapolis earlier this year. Many other ICE shootings, including some that were fatal, have not ended in charges for the agents involved. Morales, 33, has served as an ICE agent for a little over a year, according to Lindenmuth. Teare said on Friday that authorities have a “significant amount of information” on Morales, and that, in his experience, law enforcement agencies would not hire someone with his background. He did not elaborate. Morales was charged with a misdemeanor in 2013 for stealing four DVDs, according to Harris County Court records. Those charges were dismissed after he paid a $270 fine and struck a plea deal. Morales unsuccessfully ran to represent Texas’ 34th congressional district in this year’s election cycle under the name “Bam Morales,” which Lindenmuth confirmed. Morales served in the U.S. Army’s 82nd Airborne Division and later as a corrections officer and law enforcement officer, he wrote in a Ballotpedia candidate survey. He wrote that his top priorities were veterans’ rights, economic issues and service guided by the Christian principles of “compassion, integrity, service, and accountability.” He listed illegal immigration as one of the country’s greatest challenges. Morales also wrote in the survey that he was endorsed by an organization called “Make America Godlier Again.” Morales appeared at a 2024 Christian conference held by televangelist Johnson Suleman. In video of the conference, Morales appears to act as a Spanish translator as Suleman serves free food and “extends his touch of love to migrants.” “I want to pray for the immigrants,” Suleman said, as Morales translated those words into Spanish. “I bless you. May the lord grant your request and open your doors.” Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

articles.title: Mamdani says Trump agreed to grant visa for Ghanaian mom of slain Bronx teen

President Trump has agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a 15-year-old Bronx boy who was shot to death on his way to school, allowing her to travel from Ghana to NYC to mourn her son in person, NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Saturday. “The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away,” the mayor said on X. “Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. Frimpong had recently immigrated to the US from Ghana — and was being bullied at 329 The DreamYard Preparatory School, according to his father, Thomas Frimpong, 60, who told The Post he believes it is tied to the slaying. Police have not named a shooting suspect or said anything about a motive. articles.description: Rubio says the US government did not facilitate Bolsonaro’s flight to the US AP News Trump says Flavio Bolsonaro can stay in US as long as he wants Reuters Why Miami Is a Destination for Latin America’s Political Exiles The New York Times How Bolsonaro Fled Brazil: Decoys, a Private Jet and a Friend in the White House WSJ Former Mossad agent assisted Flavio Bolsonaro's escape from Brazil via Argentina - report The Je
articles.content: ATLANTA (AP) — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that the Trump administration did not facilitate defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro’s departure to the U.S. after he left Brazil following his election defeat to Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro arrived in Miami on Wednesday, a day after the State Department said that Bolsonaro and his family will be granted U.S. visas after his weekend loss in a hotly contested race that bucked a trend of conservative electoral results in Latin America. “We didn’t facilitate anything,” Rubio told reporters in Atlanta, where top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies were gathered. “We had word that he had arrived in the United States. He had previously held a visa, and the president made a decision to allow him to enter the country,” Rubio said, adding that the U.S. government was not “involved directly in any of the moves that were made.” Rubio also said that he had seen Brazil’s foreign minister, Mauro Vieira, in Atlanta both on Friday and Saturday, and that he expected to see Brazilian officials again in France in November, when France is hosting a foreign ministers’ meeting. Bolsonaro refused to concede and has called the elections fraudulent, without providing evidence. His father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, also refused to acknowledge his 2022 loss to Lula and is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup. Bolsonaro, who had President Donald Trump’s tacit support in the election, is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in Brazil and had been ordered to surrender his passport after police deemed him a flight risk. The senator from Rio de Janeiro, who will lose his seat when Brazil’s new legislature begins on Feb. 1, repeated his claim that he is a victim of persecution in a livestream on Instagram Friday. In a letter on Wednesday, the 45-year-old Bolsonaro declared himself the “true president-elect of Brazil” — a term he later softened to “leader.” He compared himself — among other figures — to Charles de Gaulle, who led the French resistance to the Nazi occupation of France from London during World War II.

articles.title: Judge allows NAACP lawsuit over xAI data center pollution to move forward
articles.description: An NAACP lawsuit accuses the SpaceX-owned AI company of violating the Clean Air Act.
articles.content: A federal judge denied a motion by xAI seeking to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit accusing the SpaceX-owned company of failing to obtain permits needed to operate the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis. Suing on behalf of the NAACP, the Southern Environmental Law Center said the AI company had “installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.” It also accused xAI of violating the Clean Air Act. xAI sought to have the lawsuit dismissed, claiming that the turbines are exempt from permitting requirements because they’re mobile. The company also argued that the plaintiffs did not have the standing to sue. “Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not ‘mobile sources’ under Mississippi’s [State Implementation Plan], and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs’ claims will proceed,” Judge Debra M. Brown wrote in her decision. Focusing on xAI’s claim that these kinds of citizen lawsuits are unconstitutional, Judge Brown wrote, “Because citizen suit plaintiffs sue on their own behalf, in their own name, and seek penalties that redress harm to themselves, they are not exercising the federal government’s executive power.” TechCrunch has reached out to SpaceX for comment. articles.description: Gary Dorris, CEO of Lighthouse Sustainability, told City Pulse on Halloween that the outcry against his proposed data center may not reflect the community’s real opinions but after a blistering […]
articles.content: Gary Dorris, CEO of Lighthouse Sustainability, told City Pulse on Halloween that the outcry against his proposed data center may not reflect the community’s real opinions but after a blistering night of criticism on Friday (Oct. 30), he acknowledged that the future of a proposed data center project in Delhi Township is unclear. “We haven’t determined our future and what we’re doing here,” Dorris said. “There are multiple courses of action but I do know this site holds a tremendous opportunity for the community in some form of development and I hope that is realized and I can help realize it.” A data center meeting with a too-full capacity and no overflow accommodations in Delhi Township on Oct. 30, 2026. Photo by Mike Ellis/City Pulse The project barely got off the ground, it was first made public on Tuesday (Oct. 27). The Lansing Economic Area Partnership, a regional economic development group, went public with a $10 billion, 423-acre data center proposal for Delhi Township exactly week before election day, in a national election in which Republicans and Democrats are racing to be the best opponent of data centers. The township had already approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, which is in effect until April; developers said that would give time to shape their project, which dangled millions and millions in incentives and other benefits. Developers also said they would back off if the community said no. The response to that invitation for public response was swift and in opposition. A crowd of people waits in a vestibule area, unable to access the Delhi Township meeting about a data center in the same building. Photo by Mike Ellis/City Pulse Delhi Township officials said within hours that they hadn’t been consulted, the township withdrew from the partnership less than a day later and scheduled a special meeting days later to vote on officially opposing the project. A hastily-arranged 5:30 p.m. Friday meeting was packed and the vestibule area was chaotic, with hundreds of people including congressional candidate William Lawrence and news reporters unable to get inside or even hear the proceedings. A fire marshal enforced a 177-person capacity in the room and there were no accommodations for the crowd outside to be able to hear what was happening. A spokesperson for the township said they are working on answers to City Pulse’s questions about the meeting arrangements. The township board unanimously voted during the meeting on a simple resolution saying the township officially opposed the project and wanted LEAP to cease any work on it “due to the overwhelming amounts of negative public input received.” Officials said they had quickly gotten 350 negative comments and eight positive ones. The site is at the Holt Economic Opportunity Park near U.S. 127. Delhi Township is often referred to as the Holt area. There are housing complexes as well as active industrial sites surrounding the area. Dorris said Saturday that the meeting was indeed stacked with opponents but the community may not have had a fair chance to hear the proposal’s benefits. He said the Delhi Township manager had arranged a quick meeting for a Friday evening with a compliant board. “It was preordained by the town (manager) that this is what she wanted and I believe that honestly the governing body largely follows her lead but it’s not serving the constituants well nor the greater Lansing area.” Congressional candidate William Lawrence outside a data center meeting in Delhi Township on Oct. 30, 2026. Photo by Mike Ellis/City Pulse He said the township’s board members neglected their fiduciary duty and didn’t consider all the extra perks and taxes that the data center proposal had brought to the table. “Last night was a manifestation of a well-organized group, they have an army,” Dorris said, of the Friday meeting, “we haven’t built up our machinery to engage with the public, that is clearly something the community is not interested in doing. It’s that lack of leadership that will keep this community in its current state but it freezes out opportunity for growth and for future generations.” Courtesy Dorris said the meeting doesn’t reflect the numbers he is looking at, which show more support of the project. “I know that on the Facebook groups it was very balanced, we monitor that in a sentiment report,” Dorris said. Asked which Facebook group or groups he was referring to, Dorris said he is using online sentiment software, which is telling him that there were 30 members of the public in opposition to the data center on social media and just as many people in support of it. “When you tally up the impressions that were negative there were 30 members and there were more than that that were positive,” Dorris said. He said the site has its greatest value as a data center. “This is still an excellent site that has potential and I would agree that, at this juncture, a data center might, would be challenged, and, yes, there are other elements of recourse but maybe the community has interest in advancing something like advanced manufacturing on this site and I think that could work well,” Dorris said. “So it might be a site that’s home to something else. It’s perfectly situated for industrial development. The last industry was a gravel pit, it’s perfect. A goldilocks site.” … Data center opponents filled a meeting in Delhi Township on Oct. 30, 2026. Photo by Mike Ellis/City Pulse “This data center is different than others, Dorris said, “we’ve gone to great lengths to differentiate it. I don’t think many data centers are offering the programs we’re offering, the environmental attributes we’re offering and the community benefits we were offering. Whatever else we do on this property will likely be less than value than the data center for the community. But I think you have to respect the opportunities in advance them accordingly.” … Dozens of people spoke at a data center meeting in Delhi Township on Oct. 30, 2026. Photo by Mike Ellis/City Pulse “Given the contentious of it in the community, I will give credit for the relative civility. It was a hostile environment but at no point did I feel unsafe and for that I am appreciative,” Dorris said. “It’s the community’s loss, not mine.”

articles.title: El-Sayed Doesn’t Want Haley Stevens to Join Him at Sunday Event
articles.content: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and former opponent Haley Stevens' political union collapsed just ahead of Tuesday's Election Day finish line.Politico reports that the El-Sayed campaign wants Haley Stevens to stay away from a scheduled appearance at a Detroit church Sunday – and to avoid the campaign trail altogether, in the ramp-up to Tuesday.FOX 2 contacted a spokesperson with the campaign who confirmed the Politico report's accuracy. A request for comment was made to the Stevens' camp, but have not received a response yet. This follows a recent back-and-forth between the candidates over support for Israel. Some say the endorsement of Stevens, who represents the more moderate section of the party, is vital for the more progressive El-Sayed. A recent political ad that Stevens labeled anti-Semitic, appears to be the flashpoint of the discord.It was produced by a Rebellion PAC and produced by liberal pundit Cenk Uygur, the uncle of his campaign surrogate and controversial streamer Hasan Piker.The ad – which Stevens said in a statement she expects El-Sayed to condemn – suggests that Israel is to blame for making prices higher for Michigan families, so money can be sent to "kill Palestinians."El-Sayed's response, according to Stevens, is that his campaign is not affiliated with it. Stevens released a statement that she expects El-Sayed to condemn it at Sunday's event with South Carolina Representative Jim Clyburn, a national Democratic leader within the party."It blames our close ally Israel for everything Michiganders cannot afford," Stevens said in a statement. "The chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League called it 'a case study in antisemitism.' A disclaimer is not a condemnation, and everyone in my community knows the difference."Stevens followed up by pointing out that El-Sayed, who is a Muslim of Egyptian descent, has made similar comments on the campaign trail at rallies and in interviews.El-Sayed responded to the Stevens statement with one of his own, suggesting Stevens was the higher-funded establishment choice against his "people-powered campaign" which defeated what he claims was a historic $70 million in outside spending to fund her."So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let's all focus on the task at hand: that's beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics, putting money in pockets, and passing Medicare for All," he said.The two faced off in a hotly contested primary, barely won by the former top Wayne County and Detroit health director. The report quoted a campaign source who said Stevens appearing would only be a distraction for the campaign in the race against Republican nominee Mike Rogers."The brushoff capped a day of the two lobbing increasingly pointed statements back and forth at each other, frustrating Democrats who say the infighting risks imperiling a state the party can hardly afford to lose as they try to flip control of the Senate," Politico reported. Mallory McMorrow, a campaign surrogate for El-Sayed did not mince words criticizing Stevens in a recent CNN interview."First of all, I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing. This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes," she told Kasie Hunt. "We may very well be the state that sends the 51st Democrat to the Senate (to take the majority)."McMorrow, a current state senator who failed in her primary bid in the US Senate race, went on to say that "nobody cares about ads" but rather the affordability crisis.Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish made waves in a recent national interview, saying he supported Mike Rogers.Turkish, a civil rights attorney, said that one group of people should not be blamed for high costs. Stevens responded by telling CNN that like many families under the same roof, it is natural to have loved ones with different political opinions.El-Sayed's rival Rogers, a former longtime GOP House representative, weighed in to support Stevens, calling her a courageous leader."She was absolutely right to call on Abdul El-Sayed to denounce the Rebellion PAC ad, and she was right to call on him to apologize for espousing the same hateful ideology behind it," he said.

Why Mamdani opposes RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's NYC event
articles.content: Zohran Mamdani called the Hindu nationalist group's ideology "exclusionary" ahead of Mohan Bhagwat's New York event. But can the mayor do anything to stop it? New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he does not support an upcoming event featuring Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Hindu nationalist group Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), though he acknowledged the city likely has no power to stop it. Bhagwat is scheduled to speak Saturday at Madison Square Garden as part of what organizers are calling the "Universal Oneness Celebration," an event expected to draw around 5,000 attendees, local media reported. It is part of a broader global outreach tour tied to the RSS's centenary year, wherein Bhagwat is visiting the United States, Canada and the UK. When asked whether the event should be canceled at a press conference, Mamdani said: "I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on canceling a private event." Mamdani is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor in New York City's history. He added that his opposition to the visit reflected his role leading a city that believes in "the belonging of each and every person, no matter their color, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from." His mother is acclaimed Indian filmmaker Mira Nair. He added that he grew up with an understanding of India as "a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India." "It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision." The event is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, which says it has backing from over 135 Hindu American organizations and is meant to promote shared heritage and interfaith unity. However, several interfaith and civil rights groups – including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York – have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history. They held a news conference outside New York City Hall calling for the event to be canceled. "Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus. He leads an extremist Hindu nationalist movement that has fueled violence, exclusion and fear for minority communities," said Sravya Tadepalli, Deputy Executive Director of Hindus for Human Rights, in a statement. "New York should not provide the RSS with a stage on which religious nationalism can be repackaged as unity." The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS, is a right-wing Hindu organization founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in 1925. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for National Volunteer Organization. The group describes itself as a "Hindu-centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus and disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance. The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization. In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video However, days earlier, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom urged sanctions against the RSS and asked the American government not to extend diplomatic courtesies to RSS members. The US government advisory body called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims." United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more. India's BJP-led government denies any discriminatory intent, pointing to programs such as food subsidies and electrification initiatives, which it says benefit all communities. The organization has been banned in India on multiple occasions, including in 1948 after a Hindu nationalist who had ties with the RSS assassinated independence leader Mahatma Gandhi. articles.content: The mouth of a sea lamprey, full of sharp, horn-shaped teeth, makes the lamprey an efficient killer of fish. (Courtesy of Karla Bartelt/USFWS)This story is made possible through a partnership between Interlochen Public Radio and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Efforts to control the invasive “coiled menace” appear to be working, according to the Great Lakes Fishery Commission. To keep the momentum going amid climate impacts, experts said continued research and investment is needed. Sea lamprey populations are down this year across almost all the Great Lakes, in line with years of slow decline of the invasive species that has harmed native fish populations. A new report from the international Great Lakes Fishery Commission says efforts to control the invasive species are working. The Canadian-American commission, working with partners across the region, has led lamprey control efforts for more than 70 years. “If you like fishing, if you like functioning ecosystems, if you like the Great Lakes, this is good news for all of us because it shows a much healthier set of Great Lakes with these invasive predators on the decline,” said Greg McClinchey, director of policy and legislative affairs for the commission. Sea lamprey are eel-like creatures that latch onto and kill native fish with their suckered mouths. Efforts to control populations typically involve barriers and applying lampricides to the rivers where they spawn before they enter the Great Lakes. Great Lakes sea lamprey numbers in 2026. (Graphic credit: Ed Ronco/IPR News) In Lake Michigan, researchers estimated 20,211 adult sea lampreys in Lake Michigan, down about 1,000 from last year. Populations in Lake Huron were at 29,602, down by nearly 15,000 sea lampreys. And Lake Superior had 29,767 of the invasive species, down more than 10,000 from the year before. Only Lake Erie saw a slight increase of 120 lamprey, but experts said those numbers are still within their target range. “It’s showing us that the things we’re doing are working, but also to find new and innovative ways to do even more,” McClinchey said. “The objective is to keep our foot on the coiled menace.” The ongoing decline comes after lamprey populations boomed during the COVID-19 pandemic, when public health guidelines restricted field work. “We saw a consequential increase in sea lamprey after that. And so this story is how they’ve closed the loop and brought it back down to the levels that we were seeing before,” said Michael Wagner, a professor of fisheries and wildlife at Michigan State University who studies sea lamprey. The most common way to bring down populations is with lampricides — chemicals that target and kill lampreys. Other strategies include installing low-head barriers or setting traps to capture lamprey. And FishPass, the selective fish passage project on the Boardman-Ottaway River in Traverse City, will sort and pass certain fish while keeping out invasive species like sea lamprey. Construction will finish next year. These efforts are working, experts said. But keeping pace with the effects of climate change will require more investment and research. From increasingly extreme floods and shifting migration patterns of the fish that lamprey attach to, “systems are becoming highly variable and less predictable,” Wagner said. Ongoing research includes looking at ways to capture sea lamprey in open rivers instead of near dams, improving lampricides in case of evolved resistance down the line, or ways to control the species without chemicals. Wagner said managing invasive sea lamprey opens up opportunities for other conservation work or tribal communities, like restoring native fish species or reconnecting rivers like the Boardman-Ottaway in northern Michigan. “It’s also important to think about the impacts that manifest from that success on people whose lives, livelihoods and cultural identity are tied to the native species we find in the Great Lakes,” he said.

articles.description: OpenAI’s latest funding round doesn't seem to be living up to expectations.
articles.content: OpenAI’s latest funding round isn’t quite living up to expectations, according to multiple news reports. OpenAI was previously reported to be raising $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation, and then at a $1.25 trillion valuation, ahead of a planned IPO. But The Financial Times reported Friday that the company has subsequently lowered its funding target to $20 billion, with a first close that’s expected to be even lower than that. The round will be led by a group of investors from the United Arab Emirates, the FT said. A subsequent retail offering for wealthy individuals could bring the total funding amount to the $20 billion target. A follow-up story in The Wall Street Journal offered more details, namely that the company has secured $11 billion so far, and that its fundraising efforts had met with a “tepid” response from some large investors. TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment. The company’s reported funding challenges could be blamed, in part, on bad timing, as Wall Street investors have become wary of heavy AI infrastructure spending, leading to a major sell off of tech stocks. And Anthropic’s planned IPO could be facing challenges, too. articles.title: It's time to 'fall back' in Michigan. When to set clocks back in 2026
articles.content: If you're staying out late on Halloween, Oct. 31, your night will end with an hour of extra sleep, as clocks are set back ahead of Daylight Saving Time's end early Sunday morning, Nov. 1. Come 2 a.m. Sunday morning, Nov. 1, the first Sunday in November, we'll "fall back," as DST ends for 2026. The seasonal time change will push sunrise and sunset each one hour earlier while, perhaps, providing an extra hour of sleep Sunday morning. While many clocks on digital devices will automatically switch with the time change, you may need to manually change some household and car clocks before going to bed this Halloween night, Oct. 31. DST will return in March 2027 as we "spring forward" once again. Here's what to know about the end of DST in Michigan this fall. Yes. Tonight, Halloween, Oct. 31, is the time to turn your clocks back, as Daylight Saving Time ends at 2 a.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, the first Sunday in November. Clocks will be set back one hour, leading to sunrise and sunset coming an hour earlier. While many digital devices like smartphones, televisions, tablets and computers automatically adjust to the time difference, you'll still need to manually change analog clocks and you may need to on digital alarm clocks or household appliance or vehicle clocks as well before going to bed Halloween night, Oct. 31, per the University of Colorado Boulder. Daylight Saving Time hasn't always ended in November. From 1987 through 2006, the fall back time change was actually set for the last weekend of October. The first time clocks fell back on the first Sunday of November was in 2007, after The Energy Policy Act of 2005 pushed the end date back by about a week. "Halloweekend" is rare. This is the first time since 2020 that Halloween and the end of Daylight Saving Time have coincided. This year will be the last time Halloween coincides with the time change or falls on a Saturday until 2037. Due to leap years, 2028, 2032 and 2036 will shift the days of the week, with Halloween skipping over Saturday for the next 11 years. According to dictionary.com, daylight saving, commonly referred to as daylight savings, "is begun in the spring by setting clocks one hour ahead. They are then set one hour back in the fall. ... People often use the simple mnemonic spring forward, fall back to remember to set clocks forward one hour (e.g., from 2 a.m. to 3 a.m.) in the spring and backward one hour (e.g., from 2 a.m. to 1 a.m.) in the fall." Daylight Saving Time is when "daylight" begins an hour later in the morning and lasts an hour longer in the evening, according to the National Institute of Standards and Technology, as we move clocks forward one hour in the spring. The clock change allows the hour of daylight to stay coordinated with the time most people are active outside. Daylight saving time is supposed to save energy, since during the warmer months the majority of people will be outside and not home, which saves energy. While it is often referred to as Daylight Savings Time, Daylight Saving Time without the "s" at the end is the correct term. No. Hawaii and most of Arizona, for instance, do not observe daylight saving time, though most states in the U.S. do. Arizona doesn’t observe it because of the state’s desert climate. The Navajo Nation, which spans parts of Arizona, Utah and New Mexico, does participate in daylight saving time. U.S. territories American Samoa, Guam, Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands also do not participate in daylight saving time. We'll spring forward at 2 a.m. on March 14, 2027, with clocks to be set one hour forward, marking the return of DST for 2027. This will make sunrise and sunset one hour later. articles.title: Harry Houdini still haunts Detroit 100 years after his Halloween death
articles.description: A century after Harry Houdini's death in Detroit on Halloween, his legendary escapes, mysterious final days and the ongoing attempts to contact his spirit continue to captivate audiences. The post Harry Houdini still haunts Detroit 100 years after his Halloween death appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: A century after Harry Houdini’s death in Detroit on Halloween, his legendary escapes, mysterious final days and the ongoing attempts to contact his spirit continue to captivate audiences. John Sherwood, left, and Scott Duck, both of the American Museum of Magic, stand beside the milk can used in Harry Houdini’s famous escape act. Duck holds a photo of Houdini performing the trick. This Halloween marks the 100th anniversary of the death of the legendary magician Harry Houdini. He earned his reputation by freeing himself from traps it often seemed no mere mortal could survive. But Houdini couldn’t escape the ultimate fate waiting for him in Detroit. And his spirit still haunts the Motor City. Harry Houdini performed in Detroit 19 times between the early days of his career in 1894 to the final show of his life in 1926. The trajectory took him from being a bottom-of-the-bill act to one of the most famous entertainers in the world. He escaped obscurity by declaring no set of handcuffs or jail cell could hold him. He dangled upside down from office buildings wearing a straitjacket, dramatically removing them in full view of those raptly watching below. Sometimes the buildings housed the local newspaper, ensuring free publicity for Houdini’s upcoming stage shows. There was always a dash of suspense involved that Houdini encouraged and sometimes inflated. In Detroit, Houdini jumped two dozen feet from the Belle Isle bridge into the frigid river below, bound with two sets of police handcuffs. He emerged unscathed, but the legend around it grew. The escape artist had leaped into a hole in ice covering the river, the story went, finding air pockets to breathe in before finally surfacing. Reports from the time show the river was not actually frozen. But that didn’t stop movies decades later from portraying it that way. As his fame grew, and a series of other magicians began copying his escapes, Houdini ramped up the stakes, stacking one increasingly death-defying feat on top of another. By 1914 he had unveiled his signature stunt, the Water Torture Cell. It was a coffin-sized box, filled with water. Houdini was lowered into it head first, both his ankles and the top of the box locked. A curtain was raised to hide the magician’s moves to escape from the audience. And even those behind the scenes, who’d seen the act many times, had goosebumps. That included Dorothy Young, who toured with Houdini as a stage assistant when she was 17 years old. “Mrs. H always stood in the wings because they had a secret code in case he couldn’t get out,” Young said. “I always watched because it was very exciting!” Young was the last surviving person to have worked with Houdini before she, too, died in 2011. A few years before, Young recalled how many movies exaggerated the circumstances of Houdini’s demise. He did not dramatically struggle to escape the torture cell. Houdini had actually been dealing with a broken ankle in the days before he traveled to Detroit. In his dressing room at a show in Montreal, Canada, a college wrestler took up the magician’s challenge that he could withstand any blow to his stomach. But the student punched Houdini several times before he could tighten his muscular midsection. “One time he showed me that he had a way of doing it,” Young said. “And to think those boys didn’t give him a chance to get himself protected.” Houdini was in severe pain and doctors advised him to rest. But he refused to cancel a series of shows already scheduled in Detroit. One of the curators at the Detroit Historical Museum, Jeremy Dimick, notes that Houdini was under financial pressure to fulfill his contract. Dimick said Houdini only made it through one performance. “He doesn’t have the strength to put his makeup on before the show and he’s kind of collapsing during the intermissions of the show. And then he has to be literally carried from the Garrick Theater back to his hotel,” Dimick said. Houdini was taken to Grace Hospital, where doctors found he’d ruptured his appendix. Several days and two surgeries later, on Halloween, Houdini breathed his last. Now the theater, the hotel, even the hospital are gone. The Detroit funeral home that embalmed him became a girls’ art school. But two decades ago, the head of the school then, Juanita Hammond, would still take visitors up a creaky set of stairs to a locked storage area with an indented floor where bodily fluids once drained. “This is the room, where it says ‘Private.’ Houdini was laid out here by the Hamilton Funeral Home in this room here,” Hammond said. It was a school Hammond said made students at the time a bit apprehensive “Some say I’m not going back to the kitchen because I might see Houdini. Ha!” The escape artist’s wife, Bess Houdini, spent years trying to see her husband again, or feel his presence. She held séance after séance searching for his ghost, though the magician himself had spent his final years exposing psychics he said preyed on the bereaved. But at a séance on Halloween a decade after her husband’s death, Bess Houdini finally said good night to Harry. She reenacted the scene in a movie a few years later, appearing in a cameo as herself. “And you remember what he always said about these things? That it was impossible for the dead to return,” she said. “This proves he was right. For if it would have been possible, I would have had some sign from him in the past ten years.” That did not stop others from trying to reach the Great Houdini in the great beyond, sometimes incorporating old pieces of his stage act. At the American Museum of Magic in Marshall, Michigan, about 100 miles west of Detroit, John Sherwood bangs on an empty, aged metal can from Houdini’s workshop. It became the centerpiece of several séances. ”That is the Houdini milk can. Houdini would jump into this while it was filled with warm water and he would be locked inside with six Mastodon locks,” Sherwood said. Like the torture cell, a screen surrounded the milk can while Houdini was staging his escape. He would invite the audience to try and hold their breath while he was doing it. After many minutes, with no sign of Houdini, the crowd would scream for them to let him out. No one could survive submerged that long. In reality, Houdini had escaped long before and would be reading a newspaper promoting his next show while the tension built. Finally, with the crowd’s anxiety at a fever pitch, Houdini’s assistants would splash him with water, since he had dried of by then, and the Master of Suspense would emerge from behind the screen, theatrically panting. Decades later, Sherwood said those holding séances he participated in would circle around the milk can and other Houdini artifacts as they tried to contact him. Sherwood said they used a special trick to coax the magician back to the land of the living. “Wanted to lure him in by essentially appealing to Houdini’s Jewish heritage by placing a lox and bagel sandwich into the milk can and invited Houdini’s spirit to take a bite out of it.” Now Sherwood is orchestrating another séance. Though previous attempts were not successful, Sherwood said the centennial of Houdini’s death might be the perfect time for the magician to appear, if for no other reason than Houdini’s sense of showmanship. “I’ve always said that the greatest publicity stunt that Harry Houdini ever pulled off was dying on Halloween. Because after that the mythology about him grew by leaps and bounds.” Was Houdini’s death certificate altered to purposely make it appear he died on Halloween? Was the wrestler who punched him a hitman sent by angry psychics to assassinate the escape artist? In some ways Houdini’s death mirrors the stunts he performed in life — shrouded in mystery.

articles.title: Caring for aging parents is getting more expensive
articles.description: Costs are soaring for people who care for their older parents and other family members, according to a new study. Out-of-pocket expenses are nearly 60% higher than they were just five years ago for family caregivers, who now spend an average of $11,508 a year on caregiving, according to a report released this week by […]
articles.content: Tennessee resident George Raines works on mobility issues with physical therapist Brad Ellis, standing, in Chattanooga, Tenn., in March 2024. A new study details soaring costs for people who care for their older parents and other family members. (Photo by Anna Claire Vollers/Stateline)Costs are soaring for people who care for their older parents and other family members, according to a new study. Out-of-pocket expenses are nearly 60% higher than they were just five years ago for family caregivers, who now spend an average of $11,508 a year on caregiving, according to a report released this week by AARP, a nonprofit that advocates for people aged 50 and older. “Whether they’re paying for groceries, housing or medical care, family caregivers are marking a significant financial commitment that can affect their own economic security,” said Debra Whitman, AARP executive vice president and chief public policy officer, in a statement. Across the U.S., 63 million people care for family members, preparing meals, managing medications, attending medical appointments and performing other daily tasks for their loved ones. The report found a 50% increase in the number of adults providing such care over the past decade. Family caregivers provide about $1 trillion in mostly unpaid labor each year, the AARP reports. They also spend thousands out of their own pockets: That $11,508 in annual caregiving spending eats up 31% of the average household income. And the burden is much heavier on low-income families. Caregivers with annual household incomes under $40,000 spend an average of 76% of their household income on caregiving, according to the report. At the other end of the economic spectrum, those with incomes above $85,000 a year spend between 9% and 19% on caregiving. Most of those caregiving dollars go toward housing and medical care, the report found. More than a third of the money spent on medical care goes toward insurance premiums, copays and direct payments to providers. Those caring for someone living with Alzheimer’s disease or another form of dementia spend more — an average of $15,846 annually. Nearly two-thirds of working caregivers reported experiencing at least one work-related disruption because of caregiving, such as having to alter work hours or take time off for caregiving responsibilities. Caregiving costs also vary depending on where a person lives. Caregivers who live in states such as New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania spend the most, an average of $15,845 per year. That’s nearly twice what those who live in midwestern states such as Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota and Missouri, who spend $7,955. The costs also vary by race and ethnicity. Asian American and Pacific Islander caregivers report the highest average spending at $16,716 (31% of average household income). Black caregivers spend an average of $13,565 annually – 52% of their household income, the highest percentage of any group. Hispanic and Latino caregivers spend an average of $10,684 per year (29%), and white caregivers reported the lowest average spending, at $9,806 per year (24%). The report’s authors recommend policy changes including tax credits, grants, paid leave for working caregivers, expanded home care options and help navigating the health care system. articles.title: Commentary: School librarians are vanishing from Michigan schools just when they are needed most
articles.description: Shannon Oltmann, Wayne State University and Kafi Kumasi Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian. Although Michigan strongly recommends that schools employ certified librarians, the state does not require them. In the 2023–24 school year, the state ranked 46th in the student-to-librarian ratio, with […]
articles.content: A new survey will evaluate school library services in Michigan. Klaus Vedfelt/Getty Images Shannon Oltmann, Wayne State University and Kafi Kumasi Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian. Although Michigan strongly recommends that schools employ certified librarians, the state does not require them. In the 2023–24 school year, the state ranked 46th in the student-to-librarian ratio, with one school librarian for every 2,760 students. The lack of school librarians impacts students across Michigan, but particularly in low-income communities like Detroit and Flint and more isolated ones like Alcona County in the northern Lower Peninsula and Ontonagon in the Upper Peninsula, exacerbating disparities in resources for young people. We are scholars in library and information sciences from Wayne State University, studying information access and ethics and equity in education and school libraries. Currently, we are conducting a statewide campaign to contact every school in Michigan and learn about their libraries, staffing, book collections, technology resources and more. Michigan’s 2025–26 School Aid budget funded our statewide survey to measure the school librarian shortage and guide efforts to address it. Our work, and the work of many others, reveals how school librarians help students become strong readers and informed citizens. Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools have a trained librarian. Harkim Wright Sr./AP Catalysts for student achievement A missing librarian is harder to see than an empty bookshelf. A room full of books can look like a school library. But if students cannot borrow those books, teachers have no librarian to plan lessons with, and no one leads author visits or digital citizenship lessons, the space offers only a fraction of what a school library can provide. School librarians bring those services to life. Also called school library media specialists, they hold a teaching certificate and complete advanced education. They connect students with books they want to read and work with teachers to build richer lessons, using library resources to extend learning beyond the textbook. Their impact stretches far beyond standardized test scores, though studies link strong library programs with higher student achievement and improved student literacy, especially for struggling readers. They can instill a love of reading and teach technological skills, which is critical in the age of artificial intelligence. At our Michigan School Census symposium held in 2026, Michigan school librarians and a principal described what that work looks like. Brian Peck, a teacher librarian at Detroit’s UPrep Academy, helped students research and build a library where none had existed. He reported that 334 students voluntarily visited and checked out books during the previous school year. At West Ottawa, librarian Julia Reynolds described replacing crowded shelves with displays that let children see book covers. Circulation quadrupled, she reported. A principal on the panel explained how district support helped schools make library visits a priority from the first week of school. Students’ information worlds Access to information is only a start. Students also need help making sense of what reaches them through searches, social media and AI. AI can create convincing fake videos of students doing or saying things they never did, harming their reputations and undermining trust in what people see online. Less visible forces shape students’ information worlds, too. Algorithms and online platforms often dictate which search results and suggested videos appear first. Students need to understand that the first result is not necessarily the most credible or trustworthy source. AI is becoming so prominent that even elementary school students are learning about it. Building information literacy Information literacy means knowing how to find, judge and use information. School librarians turn those skills into practice. For a history assignment, a librarian might help students compare a newspaper account with a firsthand record. Who produced each source? What might explain their different accounts? The same habits apply to AI. Students can trace a claim to its source, check whether the source exists and compare what it says with the generated answer. A confident response still needs evidence. Guided by certified school librarians, students can build upon these foundations and learn to effectively find, evaluate and use information, including news articles about a historic event for a social studies assignment or to analyze current social media trends. Students can also judge the accuracy, recency and relevance of information. They learn to apply information in decision-making, writing and other forms ofy communication. Becoming savvy digital citizens Knowing whether information is trustworthy is an important skill. Deciding what to do with it is another. Digital citizenship includes deciding whether to post someone’s photo, seeking their permission before doing so, and choosing not to share a fake video. Recent research emphasizes that digital citizenship prepares students to be empowered online and act ethically, safely and legally in digital environments. Our work also starts with the knowledge young people bring to school. Project Restoring Urban School Libraries helped classroom teachers earn the additional endorsement needed to become school librarians. The program combined mentoring with coursework that drew on students’ cultures, including using hip-hop to explore how young people find, create and share information. Students start by examining the media they already use. A lesson might ask them to trace a sample, credit its creator and discuss what changes when someone else’s work reaches a new audience. Fighting for recognition Principal preparation programs can help school leaders understand what school librarians contribute beyond book checkout. But principals and school librarians often train in separate academic units: colleges of education and schools of library and information science. Without shared coursework or joint projects, principals may complete their training without learning how to work with a school librarian. In our “Closing the Literacy Gap” symposium, we brought school librarians and administrators together on a panel to show what their partnerships make possible. West Ottawa Principal Audra Bolhuis joined school librarian Julia Reynolds and compared a librarian to “an instructional coach.” She described someone teachers can turn to for resources and help with classroom projects, extending the librarian’s role beyond students’ scheduled library visits. School library jobs remain vulnerable to budget cuts, and the number of school librarians across the state has been decreasing since 2010. To understand what schools provide and where support is missing, we launched the state-funded Michigan School Census in September 2026. By Oct. 21, 1,054 schools – about one-third of those invited – had completed it. Our public response map tracks participation across districts. Schools without libraries or librarians are essential to painting the full picture: Their staff can explain how students get books and research help when those services are absent. The findings will guide recommendations for staffing, resources and funding. Counting what schools have is the first step toward deciding what every Michigan student should be able to count on. Read more of our stories about Detroit and Michigan. Shannon Oltmann, Associate Dean of Information Sciences, Wayne State University and Kafi Kumasi, Professor of Information Sciences, Wayne State University.
