articles.title: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
articles.description: A long flight home from feeding grounds messes with birds' internal clocks.
articles.content: Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it's the middle of the night while the clock says it's lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans. A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass. Clockwork compass Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales.Read full article Comments

articles.title: WMU fraternity suspended. How it's tied to fatal Mattawan crash.
articles.content: In the wake of a crash that killed two Mattawan High School students, Western Michigan University issued a cease-and-desist letter to a fraternity on its campus requiring it to halt all activities while the university investigates its potential involvement. "Western Michigan University is deeply saddened by the tragic crash that claimed the lives of two Mattawan high school students," university spokesperson Paula Davis said via email on Thursday, Oct. 29. The letter, sent to Phi Sigma Kappa on Oct. 24 prohibits the student organization from all organizational activities as the investigation remains ongoing. The fraternity chapter and national organization did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the letter. Ven Johnson Law said the girls may have been attending a fraternity party the night of the crash, but did not ID the fraternity. The firm is representing the family of Aurora Ruckert, 16, who died as a result of the crash. "Ven Johnson Law represents Aurora’s family and is investigating reports that the teens, ages 15 to 17, may have attended a Western Michigan University fraternity party and been served alcohol that night," the firm said in a Facebook post. "If you have photos, messages or any information about the crash or the events leading up to it, we urge you to call us at 855-836-3444." The fraternity suspension, university officials say, was enacted in response to a notification from the fraternity's national headquarters. The school did not specify what notification the national organization provided. "We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families and loved ones of those who died. Our thoughts are also with those who were injured, and we wish them a full recovery. The University has been made aware of questions involving a fraternity and has issued a cease-and-desist directive suspending the fraternity's activities while the matter is reviewed." Two Mattawan High School students were killed and three others critically injured in a crash early Sunday morning, Oct 18, in Kalamazoo County's Texas Township. A 16-year-old and a 15-year-old were pronounced dead at the scene, the Kalamazoo County Sheriff's Office said in a release. A 15-year-old and a 17-year-old were in critical, but stable condition, and a 16-year-old was in "very" critical condition, shortly after the crash, the Kalamazoo County Sheriff's Office said. The five teens were westbound on West R Avenue near South 2nd Street just before 3:30 a.m. when the vehicle they were in left the south side of the road and crashed into a tree. In a Facebook post, Texas Township Fire Rescue said the car caught fire after the crash. Several of the girls involved were identified by family, friends and an attorney's office in the wake of the crash. A Gofundme account seeking $20,000 said two of the teens, Jordyn Bigham, 15 and Jadisson Bigham, 16, were sisters. "(Jordyn's) older sister, Jada, survived the crash but suffered severe injuries and is currently fighting in critical condition in the hospital. She faces a long, difficult road to recovery ahead, requiring extensive medical treatments, surgeries, and ongoing care," the fundraiser information provided by Steve Nelson says. "Their mother is now carrying a heavy burden that no parent should ever have to face: mourning the loss of one daughter while standing by the hospital bed of another." Additionally, a second Gofundme account identified Liyra Fuller. "Please help the Fuller family through this heartbreaking time. Their daughter, Liyra Fuller, is one of the girls in critical care after the Mattawan car crash over the weekend," Gofundme account creator Megan Deneau said. "Right now, the family is focused on being by Liyra’s side and supporting her through this critical time. Along with the deep emotional toll this has taken, they are also facing medical expenses." Ven Johnson Law said it was representing the family of Aurora Ruckert, 16, who died as a result of the crash. "Ven Johnson Law represents Aurora’s family and is investigating reports that the teens, ages 15 to 17, may have attended a Western Michigan University fraternity party and been served alcohol that night," the firm said in a Facebook post. Media reports say the fifth girl has been released from the hospital, but her identity has not been announced. Jalen Williams is a trending reporter at the Detroit Free Press. Contact him at jawilliams1@freepress.com.

articles.title: The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.
articles.description: The regulator says Tavneos was approved on the basis of manipulated study data. Should patients still have access to it?
articles.content: In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies? Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.” At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects.Read full article Comments

articles.title: CNN This Morning
Daylight saving time 2026 ends Sunday: Clocks fall back as permanent DST stalls
articles.description: Daylight saving time ends Sunday, Nov. 1. Here is when to set clocks back, the history of the time change, and where permanent daylight saving time bills stand.
articles.content: Rotunda east door clock in the U.S. Capitol( U.S. Architect of the Capitol)November is approaching, and with it approaches a familiar timekeeping tradition. At 2 a.m. on Sunday, November 1, clocks will “fall back” an hour, switching the country from daylight saving time to standard time and giving millions of Americans an extra hour of sleep.Seasonally shifting the time has been largely standardized across the U.S. for decades; every state does so except Hawaii and Arizona (barring the territory of the Navajo Nation), who both stick to standard time.Federal law does not currently allow states to opt into year-round daylight savings time, though many states have expressed a desire to do so.Daylight saving time will begin again on Sunday, March 14, 2027, when clocks “spring forward” one hour.Phones and most digital timekeeping devices will switch automatically, though older and more analog clocks will have to be manually reset.Why does the U.S. have daylight saving time?Daylight saving time was first proposed in 1895 by New Zealand entomologist George Hudson as a way for people to enjoy more hours of sunshine during the summer. Many European countries adopted it during the first World War as a way to save fuel, and the U.S. followed suit in 1918.While the U.S ditched daylight saving time nationally in 1919 after the end of the war, some states kept it around and grew fond of the system. It was re-introduced nationally decades later, when President Lyndon Johnson signed the Uniform Time Act of 1966 into law.The nation’s current system, minor tweaks to start and end dates notwithstanding, originates from this law.Many Americans want permanent daylight saving timeNowadays, daylight saving time is a frequent target of complaints for a large number of Americans who dislike having to change their clocks and circadian rhythms twice a year. A 2025 AP-NORC poll found that only 12% of Americans favor the current daylight saving system. 40% were ambivalent, and 47% outright opposed it.When asked what system they would like to see instead, 56% said they preferred permanent daylight saving time, which would extend daylight hours in the evening at the expense of a darker morning. 42% preferred permanent standard time, meaning more light in the morning and an earlier sunset.Could the U.S. end its current daylight saving time system?America’s biannual changing of clocks has gained renewed attention with The Sunshine Protection Act of 2025, a bill which would end the twice-yearly switching by permanently setting the nation’s clocks to daylight saving time. It passed the House of Representatives in July of last year, but has since stalled in the Senate.The Senate’s opposition is not without historical precedent; a law enacting permanent daylight saving time was passed through Congress and signed by President Richard Nixon in January 1974 in an attempt to save energy during an ongoing oil crisis.The change was popular at first, but public support plummeted through the winter; some parts of the country didn’t see sunrise until 9:00 a.m. The law was repealed later that year.The current bill has been the subject of conflict between President Donald Trump, who supports it, and the group of Senate Republicans who oppose it, notably Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Earlier this month, Trump posted Cotton’s personal phone number online, encouraging his supporters to dial the senator and tell him to “GET IT DONE,” in reference to the bill.With the Senate in recess and the midterm election only days away, it seems unlikely that the bill will pass any time soon. Unpassed legislation must be reintroduced to the Senate after each election.CORRECTION: An earlier version of this story reported permanent standard time would result in a later sunset, it would, however, result in an earlier sunset.

Michigan population steady at 10.1M. Detroit, Grand Rapids up slightly
articles.description: The US Census Bureau released data from its annual survey of American households this week, which included income levels and whether residents had an electric vehicle, among a variety of topics.
articles.content: This story also appeared in Bridge Michigan New US Census Bureau data shows a tiny decrease in state population Median household income increased, but trails the nation Among other takeaways: Electric vehicle ownership in Michigan is also below the national average, with about 148,000 households owning an EV Michigan’s population held steady last year, while four of the state’s 17 largest cities saw modest increases, according to newly released data by the US Census Bureau. The Census Bureau estimated that Michigan had about 10.1 million residents in 2025. It lost about 12,575 people, a drop of less than half a percent from 2024, when the state marked two years of estimated population growth. Michigan’s two largest cities, Detroit and Grand Rapids, both inched up 0.5% in population — adding 3,413 and 1,049 people respectively. But Lansing saw the biggest gain among large cities. It added 1,317 new residents, boosting its population by about 1.2% from 2024. Detroit’s estimated population last year was 649,115. Grand Rapids remained the second largest city in the state with its 201,180 estimated population, and Lansing’s increase took it to 114,783, the sixth largest in Michigan. Dearborn, Southfield, Rochester Hills and Farmington Hills each lost around 800 residents, but their estimated populations all remain larger than 75,000. The annual American Community Survey looks at a wide variety of characteristics – from educational attainment to income to transportation – to provide national and statewide estimates as well as estimates for areas with more than 65,000 residents. Here are some key takeaways: Income While the median household income in Michigan increased from $72,389 in 2024 to $75,832 in 2025, the state still trails the national median household income of $84,780, according to Census data. EVs and solar panels The survey, for the first time, included data on households that have an electric vehicle or solar panels. In Michigan, an estimated 148,819 households, or about 4%, had an electric vehicle last year, a rate that came below the 5.5% national estimate. Among nearby states, Michigan trailed Illinois and Minnesota in the percentage of households with an electric vehicle. “Western states have led the way in switching to electric vehicles,” Tricia Holley, a survey statistician at the Census Bureau, said in a news release. “California overall had the highest rate of EV adoption per household, followed by Washington, Hawaii and Nevada. The Census estimated that 65,918 Michigan households were equipped with solar panels in 2025, which trailed Illinois and Ohio, which had 177,113 and 72,125, respectively. Education Michiganders with a high school diploma or equivalent stood at 92.7% in 2025, higher than the 90.6% national estimate. However, when it comes to the portion of the population to earn a bachelor’s degree or higher, Michigan’s 33.9% estimate was below the 37.4% seen across the country. Michigan’s struggles with postsecondary degrees have persisted for nearly a decade. According to data on SAT scores released earlier this year, only a fourth of 11th graders in the state are college ready, a slight dip from 26.6% the year prior. A decade ago, it was 35%. Matt Mencarini is a Report for America corps member who covers data and accountability for Bridge Michigan.

In 28 years of walking, Karl Bushby has overcome jungle, desert and red tape. Now he's nearly home
articles.content: MARKET RASEN, England (AP) — Karl Bushby has spent 28 years walking home, but as he approaches the finish Monday, it’s not clear he’s ready for the audacious journey to end. Pushing a cart loaded with camping gear up a busy country road in northern England about 50 kilometers (30 miles) from the finish line, Bushby was uncertain of the future, anxious about the prospect of living in his mom’s basement and facing an identity crisis. British adventurer Karl Bushby walks near Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, England, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, on the final stretch of his 28-year walk around the world to get back to his mother’s home in Hull. (AP Photo/Brian Melley) British adventurer Karl Bushby walks near Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, England, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, on the final stretch of his 28-year walk around the world to get back to his mother’s home in Hull. (AP Photo/Brian Melley) “My purpose and reason for living is about to end,” he said. “It’s going to be difficult … trying to blend back into a society that you just don’t know anymore.” Bushby, 57, was just shy of 30 when he entered the unknown at the tip of South America on Nov. 1, 1998. Since then, he has walked 31,000 miles (50,000 kilometers) across four continents, navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam — a generous description of his technique — across the Caspian Sea and English Channel. He has battled almost every type of element and terrain imaginable through 30 foreign countries to get back to where he started half a lifetime ago. Swampy jungle, scorching desert and frozen tundra slowed him down, but mountains of red tape helped turn what was supposed to be a 12-year trek into the epic he has dubbed the “Goliath Expedition.” It’s taken nearly three times as long for Bushby to return to his mother, Angela, in Hull, as it took the hero in “ The Odyssey ” to make it back to his wife, Penelope, in Ithaca. “Odysseus was a bit of an amateur,” Bushby quipped. “But, you know, I’ll cut him some slack — I haven’t met any giant Cyclops.” British adventurer Karl Bushby pauses near Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, England, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, on the final stretch of his 28-year walk around the world to get back to his mother’s home in Hull. (AP Photo/Brian Melley) British adventurer Karl Bushby pauses near Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, England, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, on the final stretch of his 28-year walk around the world to get back to his mother’s home in Hull. (AP Photo/Brian Melley) The real world provided plenty of menaces of its own: there was a standoff with a polar bear; he floated through crocodile-infested waters to avoid a guerrilla war in Colombia; a mob attacked him in Peru; and he was rescued by helicopter from an ice floe drifting out to sea. The former British paratrooper’s mission was sparked by a birthday card from his father, Keith, in the mid-90s. Keith, an Army veteran himself, mentioned an argument special forces troops once had about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels. Bushby drew a continuous line on a map across Europe and Asia to North America and — instead of going to New York — carried on straight down to the tip of Chile. “And that was it,” he said. “With that under my skin, there was no going back.” Explorers have long circled the planet by boat, plane, balloon, bicycle and even on foot. But most walkers have relied on transport to cross oceans. Bushby imposed two strict rules for his journey: transportation could not be used to move forward and he had to return home on foot. He set out with $500 and soon found himself fighting hurricane-force winds on the Patagonian Steppe. He dodged war in the dangerous Darién Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America, in 2001 and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama. After being airlifted to safety during the 56-mile Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, he had a near-death plunge into freezing waters and they nearly lost all their supplies. After managing the rare crossing, they were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally. British adventurer Karl Bushby walks near Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, England, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, on the final stretch of his 28-year walk around the world to get back to his mother’s home in Hull. (AP Photo/Brian Melley) British adventurer Karl Bushby walks near Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, England, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, on the final stretch of his 28-year walk around the world to get back to his mother’s home in Hull. (AP Photo/Brian Melley) It took almost 10 years to get through Russia because of visa issues and weather that only allowed travel a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork. With each setback, he would retreat to the U.S. or Mexico, where living was much cheaper, and wait for his next chance to return to the point where he left off. He was trailed by police through China, had a lengthy setback from the pandemic and was forced to swim 31 days across the Caspian Sea because geopolitical problems had closed off Russia and Iran. He is not a good swimmer and relied on a flotation vest and wetsuit as he plodded backward by flapping his arms in a technique he calls “floatimming,” a hybrid of floating and swimming. Europe presented its own challenges, with 90-day limits on visits that forced him to travel in three-month chunks. Romance has also intervened. He spent seven years with a Colombian woman, and three with a woman from Japan. Each relationship ended in heartbreak that seemed fated by such an itinerant lifestyle. It’s been tough on his family. Bushby has a son from an early marriage to a Belfast woman that ended in divorce. His son mostly grew up without him and is now in his mid-30s. His father met him on the beach in Dover when he crossed the channel, but Bushby hasn’t seen his mother in a decade, which adds to the trepidation about his return. He has been helped by a shifting group of sponsors that have come and gone as the trip dragged on and fortunes tumbled in the 2008 financial crisis. For the past 16 years, he has relied mainly on a production company founded by “House of Cards” creator Beau Willimon and music producer Jordan Tappis, who are backing a documentary in the works by filmmaker Werner Herzog. British adventurer Karl Bushby walks near Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, England, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, on the final stretch of his 28-year walk around the world to get back to his mother’s home in Hull. (AP Photo/Brian Melley) British adventurer Karl Bushby walks near Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, England, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, on the final stretch of his 28-year walk around the world to get back to his mother’s home in Hull. (AP Photo/Brian Melley) It has been the kindness of countless strangers, though, that has buoyed and propelled him throughout, particularly from those who have the least to offer. He’s been welcomed into shacks assembled from car parts, nursed back to health from a bad stomach infection by a Peruvian doctor’s family, and fed countless meals of just rice and water by people seeking nothing in return. “I’ve been welcomed in by the poorest of the poor,” he said. “I’ve met 99.9999% of the very best of humanity. Every culture, every country has been the same response.” There have been endless stretches of loneliness that have made his final push almost surreal as word spreads of his passage through the rolling green fields that lead to his native Yorkshire. Big rigs literally blowing past him on the road near the town of Market Rasen on Wednesday tooted their horns, drivers waved and a group of motorcyclists stopped to take selfies. Howard Denton pulled his car over and couldn’t understand how a couple of cyclists he had spoken with briefly hadn’t taken note of their fellow traveler. “I said to them, ’Did you see that bloke who’s walked around the world?’” Denton said. “They said, ‘No.’ They didn’t think of asking him where he was going. I just couldn’t believe how stupid they were. I think he’s incredible. I think he’s amazing.” When Bushby started out, he looked like Kurt Cobain and even inspired an internet mock conspiracy that the late Nirvana leader was still alive, and walking around the world under a pseudonym. He’s more weathered today, softer in the midsection and has a salty beard. But his bright blue eyes, blond hair and tan belie his age. British adventurer Karl Bushby pauses during his walk near Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, England, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, on the final stretch of his 28-year walk around the world to get back to his mother’s home in Hull. (AP Photo/Brian Melley) British adventurer Karl Bushby pauses during his walk near Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, England, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, on the final stretch of his 28-year walk around the world to get back to his mother’s home in Hull. (AP Photo/Brian Melley) He may not know what lies ahead but one thing is certain: he won’t miss the thousands of steps he takes each day. “I’m not doing it because I like walking,” he said. “It’s a means of getting somewhere.”

Closing Remarks by Dr Adham Ismail, officer in charge WHO Eastern Mediterranean: Progress report on health issues facing populations affected by disasters and emergencies, including implementation of the International Health Regulations (2005)
articles.content: On behalf of the Regional Director, thank you to the Secretariat for this report, and to Member States for your interventions. What this report makes clear is that our Region’s emergency landscape is not easing — it is becoming more complex. Fourteen graded emergencies, eight of them at the highest grade: more than a third of the global total. Protracted conflicts, recurrent outbreaks, climate shocks, and relentless attacks on health care are converging with a shrinking funding envelope. Our emergency response remains more than 40% underfunded against a requirement of US$ 633 million. In 2025, funding constraints hit 1,950 WHO-supported health facilities — more than half suspended operations, affecting 25.9 million people across seven countries. We cannot manage this by continuing to lurch from one crisis to the next. We have to build something more durable. That means, first, sustaining investment in IHR (2005) implementation — particularly at points of entry, in laboratory systems, and in chemical and radiation event readiness, where capacity gaps remain widest. Second, it means embedding collaborative surveillance and public health intelligence, including the responsible use of AI, as standard practice across the Region. Third, it means an uncompromising stance on the protection of health care. In the first half of this year, the Region accounted for nearly half of all WHO-verified incidents worldwide. Health workers, patients, and facilities cannot continue to bear the cost of conflicts they did not start. And fourth, it means shifting toward national ownership and resilience — building recovery into planning from the outset, and replacing appeals made crisis by crisis with sustainable, flexible financing. None of this is the Secretariat’s task alone. It requires sustained political commitment from this Committee, and the Secretariat stands ready to support every Member State in turning that commitment into practice. We know the model delivers: in Somalia, cholera deaths fell from 135 to nine in a single year.

articles.content: ZAMORA, Spain (AP) — For decades, Spaniards have been avid users of the country’s touted high-speed trains, choosing the Ave, Spanish for “bird,” over driving or flying for work trips or holidays each year. But two devastating collisions in nine months that killed more than 100 people have shaken confidence in a rail network long hailed for its speed and safety. Two days after a train collision in central Spain killed 69 people and stunned the nation with horrific images of shredded carriages and bloodied survivors, an Associated Press journalist spoke to travelers who had decided to keep traveling by train. “I have to travel for work and am taking the train because I don’t have another option, but I have colleagues who are going by car and won’t take another train until something really changes,” Carla Fuentes, a 37-year-old economist, said before boarding in Madrid for Alicante, in southern Spain. Fuentes’ train was canceled on Thursday due to a strike by train workers to demand improved rail safety. “It is understandable,” she said about the strike. “Many lives were lost and there are a lot of people who are angry.” The catastrophe was impossible to forget once aboard the train from Madrid to Zamora on Friday, even if most of the passengers were philosophical about whizzing along at 300 kph (186 mph). Once the train started after a 50-minute delay, the train conductor made an announcement to thank those who had stuck with the Ave. “I only have words of thanks for your patience and admiration for your decision to continue traveling by train at this time,” he told the passengers. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who faces an election in four weeks, acknowledged Friday at the crash site that authorities must work hard to restore the reputation of the rail service. “Trust in our high-speed railway has been broken, and the job of this government is to not only understand what went wrong but to offer the solutions so that a tragedy of this magnitude never happens again,” Sánchez said. The crash in the province of Toledo came just nine months after another collision further south on the same Madrid-Seville line killed 49 people when one train jumped the track and slammed into another coming from the opposite direction. “I have spent a long time traveling in high-speed trains, but now my confidence has been hurt a bit,” 56-year-old traveler María Rodríguez said on the train to Zamora. “Two accidents in one year, with a lot of casualties. That is serious.” High-speed trains have transformed Spain, sharply reducing commutes between Madrid in central Spain and major cities, many of them located on the coast. Since opening its first high-speed line in 1992, Spain has laid 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of high-speed track for its 49 million residents. Only China — with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people — has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways. The union defines high-speed trains as those traveling at more than 250 kph (155 mph). It is now the most common mode of travel for both business and pleasure. Nine million of the 13 million trips made between Madrid and Barcelona in 2024 were made by high-speed rail, according to the Spanish National Markets and Competition Commission. Rail travel is growing: The number of high-speed train passengers in Spain doubled between 2019 and 2025. On an old, slow train, the 600-kilometer (385-mile) journey between Madrid and Barcelona used to take around seven hours, meaning many business travelers opted to take a plane. Now that trip can be done in 2 ½ hours. Shorter travel times have made day trips between many Spanish cities possible. But Spain’s enormous investment in building high-speed rail has come at the expense of slower commuter services, while train workers’ unions argue that the administration has not spent enough on maintaining the network. Adrián Blaya, a 29-year-old data analyst traveling on the Zamora-Madrid line, echoed the common complaint that the service has worsened in recent years with delays and breakdowns becoming habitual. Ironically, he felt safer than usual following the deadly crash. “The safest time to travel in Ave is after a tragedy because this is when they are extra careful,” he said. “Today I feel safer traveling because I know they will be focused.”
